bridge.Honolulu, an easy-going town: The ship is tied up, and the music on the pier fades away. Let's take a slow walk into town together. Can you smell the flowers on the warm air?
bridge.The fleet comes to Hawaii: Out beyond the town, past the cane fields, lies a wide, calm harbour. If you look closely, you'll see grey shapes resting on the water.
bridge.A day aboard a battleship: The sun has set over the harbour. Tomorrow, you and I will spend a whole day on board one of those great grey ships.
bridge.Dorie Miller, a farm boy from Texas: Among the thousands of young men on those ships was one quiet giant from Texas. I'd like you to meet him.
bridge.Liberty in Honolulu: When the work was done, the sailors couldn't wait to get ashore. Shall we follow them into town on a day off?
bridge.A world far away at war: The bands play on, and the island feels peaceful. But far beyond the horizon, the world was already at war. Let's look out there for a moment, gently.
bridge.The last Saturday: Back in Hawaii, December has come, warm and green. You'd hardly guess it was winter at all.
bridge.A soft Sunday dawn: The music has ended, and the moon shines on the quiet harbour. We'll go very gently now, into the morning that followed.
bridge.Two hours in December: We'll only touch the next part softly, you and I. It's sad, and we'll keep it brief.
bridge.Courage and kindness: The sky is quiet again. And in the hours that followed, you'd have seen people helping one another everywhere you looked.
bridge.After the long night: That night, the whole island was dark and still. So how did Hawaii, and the people you've met, carry on afterwards?
bridge.Their lives, and Pearl Harbor today: The years went by, and the harbour healed slowly. So what became of them all, and what would you find if you went there today?

voor.In 1941, Hawaii was not yet a state: Picture yourself leaning on the rail of a big white ship, with nothing but blue ocean all around you.
voor.When a passenger ship arrived: You'd hear a band playing on the pier long before the ship was tied up.
voor.On Oahu, it rained while the sun: You'd feel a soft, warm shower on your arms, and look up to see blue sky.
voor.More than a third of the people: You'd hear many languages on a single walk through town.
voor.The old Hawaiians divided their island: You could walk from the cool green mountains all the way down to the sea without leaving one slice.
voor.In the plantation camps, the smell: You'd hear children laughing between the little wooden houses.
voor.The Hawaiians called the harbour: You'd see why, if you stood at the water's edge at sunrise.
voor.The old palace of the Hawaiian kings: You'd stand in the shade of the banyan trees and look up at its tall windows.
voor.In Chinatown, the morning market: You'd smell fresh fish, ginger and ripe mangoes all at once.
voor.The most famous surfer in the world: If you'd met him on the beach, you'd have found him calm and kind.
voor.The grandest hotel at Waikiki: You'd walk into its cool lobby and hear the waves through the open doors.
voor.Most families in Honolulu lived: You'd sit on the porch in the evening, listening to the rain on the tin roof.
voor.The sliding sound of the steel guitar: You'd hear it drifting from radios all over town.
voor.The great American fleet had only moved: You might think the ships had always been there. They hadn't.
voor.The navy's destroyers were tied up: You'd see them lying together like sleeping whales.
voor.In the middle of the harbour lay: You'd see children cycling along its quiet roads.
voor.The battleships were named: If you came from Arizona or Nevada, you'd feel a little proud.
voor.The Navy Yard at Pearl Harbor: You could buy a stamp, see a film and get a haircut without leaving the yard.
voor.The children of Ford Island: You'd hear them calling out the names as the ships came in.
voor.At sunset, the harbour turned: You'd sit on the shore and watch the colours change, slowly.
voor.A battleship's day began: You'd be woken by that bugle, whether you liked it or not.
voor.The ship's cooks got up: You'd smell fresh bread drifting through the passageways before dawn.
voor.Every morning, sailors scrubbed: You'd kneel on the deck with the others, pushing the stone back and forth.
voor.A battleship had its own barbers: You could find almost anything you needed without ever going ashore.
voor.Every battleship had its own band: You'd hear them practising on deck in the afternoons.
voor.On Sundays, the chaplain held: You'd sit on a bench on deck, with the sea breeze in your face.
voor.In the afternoons, some sailors: You'd lean over the rail with a line and wait.
voor.In the evenings, the sailors watched: You'd sit on the deck with hundreds of others, looking up at the screen and the stars behind it.
voor.Dorie Miller grew up on a cotton farm: You'd find him in the fields with his brothers, under a hot Texas sun.
voor.When Dorie joined the navy: You might think he could choose any job he liked. He couldn't.
voor.Dorie was the heavyweight boxing champio: You'd see the crowd gather around the ring on deck to watch him.
voor.Dorie dreamed of going home: You can picture him, leaning on the rail, thinking of fields and open sky.
voor.When a sailor had a day off: You'd climb down into a little launch and feel it bob across the harbour.
voor.On Hotel Street, a sailor could have: You'd sit in the pretend cockpit and grin for the camera.
voor.Some sailors rented bicycles: You'd feel the wind in your face as you rode along the coast road.
voor.In December, sailors mailed home: You can imagine a family in a cold northern town opening that parcel.
voor.For the married men, liberty meant: You'd hear little feet running down the path to meet you.
voor.In 1941, war had been raging: You might think Hawaii was far from all that. It felt that way.
voor.Japan had very little oil: You'd need oil for every ship, plane and factory.
voor.In the first week of December, Christmas: You'd smell the pine needles as soon as you walked into the shop.
voor.Every Saturday, the captain checked: You'd hold your breath as his white glove ran along the shelf.
voor.In Honolulu, a Santa Claus sat: You'd feel sorry for him, I think, in that heavy red suit.
voor.At Waikiki, the families stayed: You'd dig your toes into the warm sand and watch the sun go down.
voor.On the last night of peace: You'd see the silver light on the water from every porch along the shore.
voor.Sunday, the seventh of December: You'd wake to birdsong and soft, golden light.
voor.Across the island, mothers were ironing: You'd hear church bells drifting across the quiet valleys.
voor.By ten o'clock in the morning: You'd hear the birds again, after a while.
voor.So many people lined up to give blood: You'd see the line stretching all the way down the street.
voor.Even little private fishing boats: You'd see them coming from every corner of the harbour.
voor.That night, every light on Oahu went out: You'd look up and see more stars than you'd ever seen before.
voor.The next day, the whole country: You'd gather around the radio with your family, quiet and listening.
voor.That Christmas in Hawaii, families: You'd sit inside with the curtains drawn, the tree glowing softly.
voor.Divers in brass helmets: You'd see bubbles rising slowly to the surface above them.
voor.The white memorial over the Arizona: If you visit, you'll take a small boat across the harbour to reach it.
voor.Every day, a few small drops of oil: Look down into the water, and you'll see them shimmering.
voor.Every year on the seventh of December: If you're there, you'll hear only the water and the wind.
